newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sets 1999 deadline for completing its market.
newsitem.headline: EU sets 1999 deadline for completing its market.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer, saying new jobs and economic growth were going to waste, threw down a new 1999 deadline for building a true European Union single market.

EU governments should plug holes in the 15-nation single market -- supposed to have been created by January 1, 1993 -- by the time the EU's single currency is created, Santer told the European Parliament ahead of Friday's EU Dublin summit meeting.
"These proposals should enter into force at the same time as the single European currency -- January 1, 1999. It's only logical," he said in Strasbourg.
"Why deprive ourselves any longer of all the dynamic advantages and job-creating potential that a properly working single market would give us?"
Santer, vowing to present proposalsto fill the gaps by next June's EU summit in Amsterdam, said: "I am convinced that we have to fix ourselves a new mobilising objective."

He said he wanted to implement long-delayed proposals to allow firms to set up as European companies, to boost the biotechnology industry and make the EU services sector perform to its full potential.
The EU needed to make progress on tax issues raised by the border-free market and to simplify rules where possible.

As Santer spoke, the European Commission announced the publication of a new book showing that the single market was beginning to create jobs, boost growth, cut inflation and improve competitiveness, but still left a lot to be desired.
The EU originally set a deadline of the end of 1992 for creating a region where people, goods, capital and services could move freely across national borders.

"Creating a single market is a historical process, not a one-off event," the commissioner responsible for the single market, Mario Monti, said in a statement. EU governments needed to make a "new commitment" to the plan.
Based on the results of 38 impact studies, the book "The single market and tomorrow's Europe" said the single market programme had produced 900,000 new jobs.
"Where would we be without the hundreds of thousands of jobs which have been created by the dynamism of the world's biggest market?" Santer asked.

The book said EU income was 1.1 percent to 1.5 percent higher in 1994 than it would have been without the single market, while inflation rates were one to 1.5 percent lower than they would have been. It said trade within the bloc was up 14 percent in manufacturing and 7.6 percent in services, without specifying a time period.
Monti said the market had resulted in lower prices, more consumer choice, higher living standards and improvements in health and safety at work, product safety and environmental protection.
But he said EU governments were not yet properly applying the rules and consumers and companies did not have adequate means of redress.

He said important rules still needed to be agreed in key areas such as energy, that the rules on public purchasing were not fully working and there was a need for more common European technical standards.
